2A.method: Form opinions in this order: (1) base_year_anchor: find strongest direct evidence—company product revenue, regulatory quotas, trade/import statistics, or named third-party supply outlooks; if only shares/spreads are available, anchor all dimensions to 2025 latest actual year and do not restate history. (2) forecast_growth_vs_history: decide whether the market has structural tailwinds (regulation, technology, underpenetration) or maturity/saturation; set forecast gap accordingly, usually +0.5 to +1.2pp, never a step-change unless clear discontinuity. (3) region_split: identify the primary demand driver—healthcare spend, manufacturing/installed base, or consumer population; use that to set NA/EU/APAC shares before looking at means. (4) region_growth: assign growth premiums/discounts based on penetration and infrastructure buildout; APAC usually premium, NA/EU discount, unless policy-driven. (5) country_split: within regions, weight by production hubs, population, reimbursement, or defense programs; use residual 'Rest of' lines for long-tail. (6) country_growth: adjust country gaps by local policy, sanctions, macro, and maturity; cross-check against the 1.3pp typical country gap standard deviation. Evidence order: direct volume/revenue > trade data > installed base > population/income > analyst convention.

2B.method: Start with use_case_split: identify 3–6 use cases from end-use/application/channel/patient group, using installed base, regulatory labels, and demand-side volume. Set the largest use case first from historical/legacy evidence, not a uniform 1/n split. Then assign use_case_growth premiums/discounts relative to the market root, using technology adoption lifecycle, regulatory/policy tailwinds, channel substitution, and maturity as primary drivers. Finally adjust use_case_mix_by_region for each region, using local industrial/demand specialization and policy/infrastructure shocks; keep shifts small (±1–3 pp) unless a documented extreme factor exists. Check that use-case shares in each region sum to 100% and that the weighted average growth premium equals the root within rounding.

pitfalls: Using growth premiums as absolute growth rates instead of adjustments to the root CAGR.
Forcing equal use-case shares when the market is concentrated; use installed base/regulatory evidence and allow one segment to be 50-80%.
Applying large regional mix shifts (+5 to +15 pp) without a specific policy or resource shock; typical region deviations are about 1 pp.
Mechanically balancing regional mix shifts by dumping residual into 'Others' without checking that the resulting shares are plausible; instead adjust all segments proportionally.
Double counting channel shifts: if you already adjusted channel use-case growth, do not also make a large channel mix shift unless it reflects geography-specific channel differences.
Copying growth premiums from one market category to another with different demand drivers (e.g., policy-driven defense vs consumer cosmetics).
Ignoring saturation: assigning high growth premiums to segments that are already large (e.g., renewable diesel/HVO) despite policy support.

2C.method: Start with the top-level type_split: identify the major types from regulation, installed base, standard of care, and technology maturity. Then set type_growth as share-shift premiums or discounts relative to the root market, making the weighted sum equal to root. After that, adjust type_mix_by_region only when there is product-specific regional evidence; otherwise hold regional shifts flat. Then split sub_segment_split within the largest parent types using installed-base or application logic. Finally set price_by_region as a consistency check, using local cost, logistics, and purchasing power; never use price to plug a volume gap. Evidence order: regulation/payer/standard; installed base and endpoint counts; substitution/adoption curves; regional income, manufacturing and logistics; historical price indices.

heuristics.condition: A split contains premium/novel and price-sensitive/legacy types, and regions differ in ability to pay, regulatory rigor, or industrial base.
heuristics.action: Shift premium/novel types +1 to +3pp in North America/Europe and price-sensitive/legacy types +1 to +3pp in APAC/LatAm/Africa. Total shift per type usually <=3pp; hold flat if no evidence.
heuristics.why: Higher income and stricter regulation pull premium/novel types toward developed regions; cost-sensitive procurement pulls commodity types toward emerging regions. Examples: azelaic pharma API NA +2, Europe cosmetic +1; high-energy laser fiber/solid NA +1, gas Africa +1; amphetamine mixed salts APAC +2; athletic tape cloth MEA +2.
markets: North America & Europe Azelaic Acid Market
heuristics.caveat: Do not shift every segment by +1/-1 just for regional flavor; globally standardized products may have zero regional shift, as in retail self-scanning product type.

heuristics.condition: Market maturity/asset age creates leapfrog or legacy adoption: developed markets already have base and shift to next-gen/system-level; emerging markets either use legacy or leapfrog to app-based/on-demand.
heuristics.action: Shift developed regions toward next-gen/distributed models by +1 to +9pp and emerging regions toward asset-level/basic/cash/on-demand by +1 to +8pp; default to ±2pp unless there is a structural reason for larger.
heuristics.why: Installed base inertia and income/technology leapfrog drive regional differences. Examples: PLC North America broadband +9, MEA narrowband +8; digital twin asset twin in MEA/LatAm +1, system twin developed; UCO route North America bulk +1, Africa on-demand +1.
markets: Global Used Cooking Oil Collection Market
heuristics.caveat: Large shifts like +9pp are outliers; many past analysts probably over-adjusted from a global average. If only one region has evidence, keep the shift <=2pp and re-check total regional shares.

heuristics.condition: Within a parent type, one application/route/form is the default and the rest are niche.
heuristics.action: Set the dominant child at 40-70% of the parent, second at 20-40%, and remaining long-tail at 5-25%. Give the dominant child 0.0 to +0.7pp growth vs parent unless it is being disrupted; the fastest niche gets +0.5 to +3.0pp; laggards get -0.3 to -2.5pp.
heuristics.why: Pareto concentration is common; the all-market top-segment mean is about 0.54. Examples: GBR 62% of dental parent, flexible PU 56% of PU, tablets 57.9% of dosage forms, electricity metering 71% of metering.
heuristics.caveat: If the category is fragmented with no default, don't force a >50% child; use several 20-30% children instead.

heuristics.condition: The parent type is asset-heavy or installed-base-driven, so child shares follow the population of installed endpoints/equipment.
heuristics.action: Assign child shares proportional to installed endpoints, e.g., electricity meters 71% of metering, in-premises CPE 75% of broadband, transformer 27% of asset twins. Give replacement-critical children +0.2 to +1.7pp and legacy children -0.5 to -2.5pp.
heuristics.why: Current revenue follows installed base; growth follows replacement/digitization. Examples: electricity metering 71%, in-premises data networking 75%, transformer 27%, circuit breaker 20%.
heuristics.caveat: If rapid new device installation is occurring, installed-based share under-estimates fast-growing children; use growth premium but don't jump share by more than 5pp without shipment data.

heuristics.condition: Regional prices reflect ability to pay, local manufacturing costs, logistics, and regulatory premium.
heuristics.action: Set North America 1.00-1.25, Europe 1.00-1.30, APAC 0.75-0.99, LatAm 0.76-1.03, MEA 0.70-1.08, with Africa often lowest at 0.70-0.97. Use Europe >1.10 for strict regulated/premium markets, North America >1.10 for specialty/pods/strong dollar, APAC <0.95 for commodity/local manufacturing. If the product is globally traded/commodity, set all regions 0.95-1.05.
heuristics.why: Prices track local income, competition, logistics and reimbursement. Examples: Athletic tape Europe 1.28 / NA 1.17 / APAC 0.84 / Africa 0.70; Decaf NA 1.25 / APAC 0.75; WFI Europe 1.20 / APAC 0.83; UCO NA 1.15 / Africa 0.72.
markets: Global Water for Injection Container Market
Global Used Cooking Oil Collection Market
heuristics.caveat: Do not use regional price index to compensate for a wrong volume split; if arbitrage/global procurement exists, e.g., collagen membrane LatAm indexes around 1.0, keep price near 1.0.

heuristics.condition: You have sub-national or small/remote market price indices.
heuristics.action: Set high-volume/competitive hubs at 0.96-0.99, remote/landlocked/small order markets at 1.02-1.13 vs the national root. Example: India SWRO South 0.99, East 1.05, Northeast 1.13.
heuristics.why: Logistics costs, order size, and competitive intensity create within-country price spreads.
markets: India Seawater Reverse Osmosis (SWRO) & High-Rejection Industrial RO Membrane Market
heuristics.caveat: Only apply sub-national if you have specific logistics/hub evidence; otherwise stay at regional level.

heuristics.condition: No product-specific regional difference in adoption or demand is known.
heuristics.action: Set all regional type-mix shifts to zero, i.e., no shift from global type shares; do not use global average region shares to force an adjustment.
heuristics.why: This is a house convention to prevent overfitting. In some past models, product type mix was flat across regions when the analyst had no evidence; however, always check whether a regional pattern exists before defaulting to zero.
markets: Global Retail Self Scanning Solutions Market
heuristics.caveat: Do not confuse 'no data' with 'no regional difference'; collect evidence on regulation, income, and local production first. If evidence exists, apply heuristic 2C-6 or 2C-7 instead.

pitfalls: Copying global average regional shares, e.g., NA 37.5%, Europe 27.1%, APAC 22.7%, as a default for every market. Actual shares vary widely; for example, chemicals APAC is 38%, high-energy laser APAC is 30%, and Europe can drop to 17%.
Applying huge growth premiums to every 'AI/sustainable/cloud/pods' niche without checking base size or revenue. Many small niches cannot sustain +5pp after they become >20% share.
Forcing a dominant segment when the market is fragmented. The average top-segment share is about 54%, but some categories have top shares of 40-45%.
Over-adjusting regional mix with large ±8/9pp shifts from a global base unless there is strong structural evidence. Such shifts are outliers and may be mechanical from a single expert.
Treating all split categories as brand/generic or OTC/Rx when devices/consumables have entirely different substitution dynamics.
Setting all price indices to 1.0 or using NA/Europe premium in commodity markets. Price should reflect local income, logistics, and competition, and should not be used to plug volume gaps.

Ignoring the base effect in type_growth: growth premium is share shift, not absolute growth. A small segment can have +6pp but still not move the market much, so do not assign big absolute size to it.

calibration.note: Market-specific evidence (installed base, OEM/shipment data, trade data, company revenues) overrides every house default band. A house_convention band is the weakest input: use it only when nothing specific is known, and say so.
calibration.source: mimic test 2026-11-10: held-out Glass Packaging (CAL-2) and the gearbox (CAL-3, so the gearbox is not fully blind on this point) showed heuristics applied outside their conditions

calibration.note: For aftermarket, service, spare-part, repair or consumable markets, the base-year split follows the INSTALLED BASE where the assets already are (cumulative past installations and their age) - not where new capacity or manufacturing is growing today. Fast new-build regions earn a growth premium, not an inflated base-year share. Choose the heuristic whose CONDITION matches the market's demand mechanism before applying its numbers.
calibration.source: mimic test 2026-11-10: held-out Glass Packaging (CAL-2) and the gearbox (CAL-3, so the gearbox is not fully blind on this point) showed heuristics applied outside their conditions

disabled_decisions.region_split: mimic test 2026-11-10: with the region-share bands the analyst's base-year geography shares got worse on held-out markets (2.86 -> 3.94 pp; calibrated 3.66 pp) and on the gearbox (3.19 -> 7.00 pp), while every other decision improved; region shares are left to market evidence (OEM installed base), growth gaps keep their heuristics
